A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RepLIn research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, figures, tables, and the code listing, allowing relocated and revised material to be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original Windmill, CelebA, CivilComments, five-variable causal-graph experiments, and synthetic simulations.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds experiments on imperfect interventions, predictor geometry, nonlinear mixing, and failure examples.

M1.justification: RepLIn retains its prediction, interventional-dependence, and self-dependence losses and its resampled variant. Expanded kernel explanations and additional experimental model configurations do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: The original datasets and tasks remain. Appendices B.4 and H.1 extend synthetic coverage to contaminated interventional training data and a controlled nonlinear-mixing family, substantially broadening the conditions under which robustness is examined.

E2.justification: The practical benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 adds an explicit robust linear oracle, defined using an entirely interventional distribution, to the predictor-weight comparison with vanilla and RepLIn predictors in Figure 15.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark settings are retained. New appendix protocols include probabilistic replacement of interventional samples with observational samples, randomized input dimensions, and nonlinear-generation experiments using two-hidden-layer MLPs and Bayesian hyperparameter selection. These are additional evaluation designs, not evidence that the original benchmarks were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds imperfect-intervention sensitivity tests, correction-vector visualizations, GradCAM cases correctly classified by ERM but missed by RepLIn, and experiments linking nonlinear mixing to loss-weight selection. The original loss-balancing analysis remains, moving from Appendix F to H.

E5.justification: Table 1 gains mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. Figure 21 reports medians and interquartile ranges for the best-performing 5% of 4,500 hyperparameter runs per nonlinearity setting. The existing five-seed benchmark policy remains unchanged; additional repetitions of retained experiments are not established.

E6.justification: New results establish imperfect-intervention failure regimes, predictor-correction behavior, nonlinear-mixing sensitivity, and adverse GradCAM examples. Table 1 also revises entries: vanilla ERM interventional accuracy changes from 58.56 to 60.15±3.12, matching the aggregate already reported in Table 2. This is not evidence of a new performance gain; the original benchmark scores are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds covariance-based oracle and ERM solutions, excess-risk expressions, and a correction-vector derivation under stated assumptions. Appendix C adds a mathematical example distinguishing predictive robustness from full identifiability. Proposition 1 and its original proof remain. The new derivation contains inconsistent parent/child indexing, limiting its clarity.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain: the dependence–accuracy association, linear-model analysis, and RepLIn. V3 qualifies the abstract, introduction, and conclusion more explicitly around known interventions and semi-synthetic causal structures in the real-data experiments.

C2.justification: V1's speculation about imperfect interventions becomes an evidence-based discussion of benefits and failures in v3. Section 6.3 also expands graph-misspecification limitations, acknowledges tuning costs, and explains when intervention-specific predictors may be preferable. New appendices interpret predictor corrections and the relationship between data complexity and loss weights.

D1.justification: V3 explicitly specifies RBF kernels for the dependence loss and documents the new simulations' noise distributions, dimensions, architectures, and hyperparameter-search procedures. The original implementation table, optimizer information, and Windmill code listing remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning against domain generalization and identifiable causal representation learning, including Appendix D and Table 7. It adds relevant literature such as Rosenfeld et al., Bing et al., and work on mutual-information estimation and kernels. The earlier reweighting discussion is relocated rather than removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem setup, method explanation, experimental narrative, and limitations undergo extensive rewriting and clearer subdivision. Related-work material is reorganized across the main text and appendices, and publication front matter and acknowledgments are added.

P2.justification: V3 adds Figures 14–16 and 20–21 and the domain-generalization comparison table. V1 Tables 7–12 become three paired observational/interventional tables in v3, with substantially smaller lettering. Existing figures and tables are also relocated and their captions revised.

improvement.justification: V3 replaces speculation about imperfect interventions with controlled evidence, adds failure examples and tuning studies, and qualifies the semi-synthetic setting more clearly. These improve transparency and applicability guidance. The original benchmark evidence remains unchanged, while inconsistent parent/child indexing in Appendix B.4 and denser appendix tables limit the theoretical and presentation gains.
